# Data Retention, Privacy & API Policies

Zero data retention conditions across Gemini Developer API, Vertex AI, OpenAI; feature-specific retention (grounding, File API, caching, interactions, abuse logging); opt-out availability; Google Cloud enterprise retention scenarios.

Google's APIs differ significantly in zero data retention (ZDR) guarantees depending on which surface you use. The key distinction is **Gemini Developer API** (AI Studio / ai.google.dev) vs **Vertex AI / Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform** (Google Cloud).

## Training restriction (Gemini Developer API)

For **Paid Services** on the Gemini Developer API, Google does not use your prompts (including system instructions, cached content, and files such as images, videos, or documents) or responses to improve Google products [1].

## Gemini Developer API — per-feature retention

| Feature | Retention | ZDR path |
|---|---|---|
| Abuse monitoring (Paid Services) | Limited period; prompts & responses logged solely to detect Prohibited Use Policy violations | Use Vertex AI if you need guaranteed ZDR or enterprise data processing agreements [1] |
| Grounding with Google Search | 30 days; prompts, contextual info, generated output; used for debugging/testing | **Cannot be disabled.** Do not use this feature if ZDR is required [1] |
| Grounding with Google Maps | 30 days; prompts, contextual info, generated output; used for reliability engineering/debugging | **Cannot be disabled.** Do not use this feature if ZDR is required [1] |
| Interactions API | Default `store=true`; conversation state retained | Set `store=false` explicitly in every request [1] |
| Live API / SessionResumptionConfig | Up to 24 hours of conversation state (text, audio, video) if a session handle is generated | Do not configure `SessionResumptionConfig` [1] |
| File API | Files stored at-rest until deleted or expired | Manually delete files; File API storage is independent of ZDR log-dropping policies [1] |
| Explicit Context Caching (`cached_content`) | Stored until user-defined `ttl` or `expire_time`; request logs follow ZDR dropping | Do not use `cached_content` for absolute ZDR [1] |
| Implicit In-Memory Caching | RAM only, project-isolated, 24-hour TTL; **not** at-rest | **Does not violate ZDR** [1] |

## Vertex AI / Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform — per-feature retention

| Feature | Retention | ZDR path |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt logging — Google models (abuse monitoring) | Limited period; governed by Section 4.3 of Google Cloud Platform ToS | Request an exception for abuse monitoring [2] |
| Prompt & response logging — Advanced AI models | Additional logging under Advanced AI Safety Addendum; ZDR **may not be possible** for some Advanced AI features | Contact your account team [2] |
| Grounding with Google Search | Up to **3 days**; queries derived from prompts + contextual info; used for debugging | **Cannot be disabled.** Use Web Grounding for Enterprise if ZDR is required [2] |
| Grounding with Google Maps | **30 days**; prompts, contextual info, generated output; used for reliability engineering | **Cannot be disabled** [2] |
| Request-response logging | Disabled by default; if enabled, writes requests/responses to BigQuery | Do not enable this feature [2] |
| Interactions API | `store` defaults to `true` for all models; stores prompts, responses, conversation state | Set `store=false` explicitly [2] |

Note the difference in Google Search grounding retention between the two surfaces: the **Developer API retains for 30 days**, while the **Enterprise Agent Platform retains for only 3 days** — but neither allows opt-out [1][2].

## Summary: achieving ZDR

- **Developer API**: guaranteed ZDR is not achievable for abuse monitoring on Paid Services. Migrate to Vertex AI for enterprise-grade ZDR controls.
- **Vertex AI / Enterprise Agent Platform**: ZDR requires opting out of or avoiding each feature above individually. Advanced AI features may block ZDR entirely — contact your account team.
- **Grounding features (both surfaces)**: storage cannot be disabled; avoid them entirely if ZDR is a hard requirement.
- **Interactions API (both surfaces)**: always set `store=false` explicitly, as the default is `true`.

## Sources

1. Zero data retention in the Gemini Developer API  |  Gemini API  |  Google AI for Developers — Web · https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/zdr
2. GOOGLE_CLOUD_GROUNDING_PRIMARY_RETENTION.md — File

# Deep Research Models, APIs & Tool Config

OpenAI o3/o4-mini and Gemini Deep Research APIs: multi-step workflows, clarifying questions, tool integration, background execution, Responses API, pricing, webhooks; Gemini built-in tools (Google Search, URL Context, Code Execution, MCP, File Search), agent config, output formatting.

## OpenAI: o3-deep-research and o4-mini-deep-research

Models `o3-deep-research` and `o4-mini-deep-research` run through the **Responses API** (`POST /v1/responses`) [1]. At least one data source tool must be included; the Responses API does not add a clarification or prompt-rewriting step automatically — the model starts researching immediately from the input it receives [2].

**Supported tools:**
- `web_search_preview` — public web search
- `file_search` with `vector_store_ids` (max 2 vector stores; only `type` and `vector_store_ids` are supported parameters) [2]
- `mcp` (remote MCP server) — must implement a `search` + `fetch` interface; `require_approval` must be set to `"never"` [2]
- `code_interpreter` — for complex data analysis

**Private data access options** (beyond web search) [2]:
- Inline in prompt text
- File search over managed vector stores (up to 2 at a time)
- Connectors (Dropbox, Gmail, etc.) — treated as built-in tools with a third-party backend
- Remote MCP server implementing search/fetch interface (generic `o3` can be used instead if full MCP tool calls are needed)

### Background mode and webhooks

Tasks can take tens of minutes [1]. Use `background=true` to decouple execution from the HTTP connection; configure a webhook to receive completion notification [1]. Background mode retains response data for **roughly 10 minutes** to allow polling, making it **incompatible with Zero Data Retention (ZDR)** — leave `background=false` if ZDR is required (OpenAI still accepts `background=true` on ZDR credentials for legacy reasons). Modified Abuse Monitoring (MAM) organizations can safely use background mode [1].

**Cost and latency control:** Use `max_tool_calls` to cap the number of tool calls (web search, MCP) the model makes. This is the primary lever for constraining cost and latency [1].

### Output structure (Responses API)

The `output` array may contain [1]:
- `web_search_call` — includes `action` (`search`, `open_page`, `find_in_page`) and status
- `code_interpreter_call`
- `mcp_tool_call`
- `file_search_call`
- `message` — final answer with inline citations; `annotations` carry `url`, `title`, `start_index`, `end_index`

Citations must be made clearly visible and clickable in the UI.

### Clarifying questions and prompt rewriting (optional pipeline)

ChatGPT Deep Research uses a 3-step pipeline; the Responses API skips steps 1–2 by default [2]:
1. **Clarification** — an intermediate model (e.g., `gpt-4.1`) gathers user intent/constraints before research begins.
2. **Prompt rewriting** — the intermediate model expands the original query into a detailed prompt.
3. **Deep research** — the expanded prompt is passed to the deep research model.

Developers can implement steps 1 and 2 manually using a faster model as a pre-pass. The Responses API only executes step 3 [2].

---

## Gemini Deep Research agent

Two versions available via the Interactions API [3]:

| Version | Model ID | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Deep Research | `deep-research-preview-04-2026` | Speed/efficiency, streaming to client UI |
| Deep Research Max | `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` | Maximum comprehensiveness, automated synthesis |

Background execution (`background=true`) is **required** for all tasks; additionally `store=True` is required because the agent uses background interactions [3][4]. Max research time is 60 minutes; most tasks complete within 20 minutes [3].

### Supported tools

Default tools (no `tools` parameter needed): Google Search, URL Context, Code Execution. Explicitly pass `tools` to restrict or extend [4]:

| Tool | `type` value | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Google Search | `google_search` | ✓ |
| URL Context | `url_context` | ✓ |
| Code Execution | `code_execution` | ✓ |
| MCP Server | `mcp_server` | — |
| File Search | `file_search` | — |

MCP Server config fields: `type`, `name`, `url`, `headers` (auth tokens), `allowed_tools` (to restrict callable tools) [4].

File Search uses `file_search_store_names` (e.g., `['fileSearchStores/my-store-name']`) [4].

### Agent configuration (`agent_config`)

Pass as a dict/object with `type: "deep-research"` required [3]:

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | required | Must be `"deep-research"` |
| `thinking_summaries` | string | `"none"` | `"auto"` streams intermediate reasoning steps |
| `visualization` | string | `"auto"` | `"auto"` enables charts/images; `"off"` disables |
| `collaborative_planning` | boolean | `false` | `true` enables multi-turn plan review before research |

### Collaborative planning (3-step flow)

1. Set `collaborative_planning=true` → agent returns a research plan (not a full report) [3].
2. Use `previous_interaction_id` with `collaborative_planning=true` to refine the plan across turns [3].
3. Set `collaborative_planning=false` (or omit) and pass `previous_interaction_id` to approve and execute [3].

### Follow-up interactions

After a completed task, pass `previous_interaction_id` with a new `model` interaction (not agent) to ask for clarification, elaboration, or summarization without restarting the research [3].

### Pricing (Gemini Deep Research)

Pay-as-you-go based on underlying model tokens and tool usage [3]:

- **Deep Research** (`deep-research-preview-04-2026`): ~80 search queries, ~250k input tokens (~50–70% cached), ~60k output tokens → **~$1.00–$3.00 per task**
- **Deep Research Max** (`deep-research-max-preview-04-2026`): ~160 search queries, ~900k input tokens (~50–70% cached), ~80k output tokens → **~$3.00–$7.00 per task**

### Limitations (Gemini)

- Custom Function Calling tools not supported; remote MCP servers are supported [3].
- Structured outputs not supported [3].
- `background=True` requires `store=True`, which is incompatible with strict zero-data-footprint requirements [3][4].
- Google Search is enabled by default and specific usage restrictions apply to grounded results [3].

### Output formatting

Gemini Deep Research output can be steered via prompt formatting instructions (sections, subsections, data tables, tone). Structured output (JSON schema) is not supported. Multimodal inputs (images, PDFs) are supported but increase cost and risk context window overflow [4].

---

## Data retention and ZDR considerations

- **OpenAI:** `background=true` retains data ~10 minutes; incompatible with ZDR. MAM projects can use background mode safely [1].
- **Gemini Developer API:** background execution requires `store=True`; this agent path does not meet strict zero-data-footprint requirements [4].
- These are distinct controls: OpenAI's ~10-minute polling window vs. Gemini's `store=True` interaction requirement are not equivalent [4].

## Sources

1. Deep research | OpenAI API § overview — Web
2. Deep research | OpenAI API § Replace the illustrative IDs and URLs below with your own resource values. › Prompting deep research models — Web
3. Gemini Deep Research agent  |  Gemini API  |  Google AI for Developers § Reconnect if the connection drops — Web
4. Gemini Deep Research agent  |  Gemini API  |  Google AI for Developers § overview — Web
5. PROVIDER_RESEARCH_STORAGE_SCOPE_2026-09-27.md — File
6. Gemini Deep Research agent  |  Gemini API  |  Google AI for Developers § Third interaction: approve the plan and kick off research › Supported tools — Web

# Sanity Knowledge Bases & MCP Access

Building and maintaining Knowledge Bases (source types, conflict resolution, refresh, rebuild); Sanity Context MCP server connecting AI agents to Sanity datasets via GROQ, read-only mode, mode and knowledgeBase parameters.

Sanity Context is a hosted, read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that gives AI agents structured access to your content — either from a live Sanity dataset (GROQ mode) or from a pre-built Knowledge Base index (Knowledge Base mode) [1]. Context MCP cannot write back to your dataset; for write tools, see the separate Sanity MCP server [1].

## Requirements

- **Context enabled for your organization.** An organization admin enables it from the Labs page (`https://sanity.io/manage/org/labs`) [1].
- **Organization API token with Context Viewer permissions.** Created under Manage > API > Tokens at the organization level (not a project read token). Viewer is the minimum; Editor also works [1].
- **An MCP-capable AI harness** (e.g. Vercel AI SDK or any MCP-speaking application) [1].
- **Knowledge Base mode additionally requires** at least one Knowledge Base that your token can read [1].

## Retrieval modes

Context serves content in two modes: GROQ mode queries the dataset at request time (suited to structured, schema-defined content); Knowledge Base mode serves a pre-built index (suited to answers spread across prose from multiple sources). The mode determines which tools the endpoint serves. For GROQ syntax details, see `sanity/groq_and_schema` [1].

Two URL query parameters switch an endpoint to Knowledge Base mode [2]:
- `mode=knowledge_base` — serves Knowledge Base tools instead of GROQ tools.
- `knowledgeBases=KNOWLEDGE_BASE_ID` — selects a Knowledge Base by its public id (begins with `kb`); separate multiple ids with commas.

For a deployed application, add the Knowledge Base as a source in the Context app instead of passing URL parameters. An endpoint whose sources are all Knowledge Bases serves Knowledge Base tools automatically [2].

## Knowledge Bases — concepts

A Knowledge Base is a pre-built index over material you choose (datasets, websites, uploaded files), belonging to an organization and able to draw from more than one project [3].

**Purpose:** Every Knowledge Base requires a purpose — one or two sentences describing its audience and job. The purpose steers the outline during a build (tagging entries `[core]`, `standard`, or `[peripheral]`) and is served to agents at the head of the outline [3].

**Outline:** A pre-generated index of every entry path with a one-line summary. Small enough for an agent to hold in context for an entire conversation. Agents use it to select the entries most likely to answer a question, then fetch those entries. Served via the `initial_context` MCP tool [3].

**Entries:** Markdown documents written from the Knowledge Base's sources, with citations back to originals. Entries belong to a build; they cannot be edited by hand. To change what a Knowledge Base says, update the source or add an instruction [3].

**Issues:** Detected when the same fact appears in multiple sources with conflicting values. The build raises a conflict rather than guessing. Coverage gaps, structural problems (missing topics, overgrown entries), and entry-removal proposals also surface as issues. Issues marked **Critical** affect facts an agent is likely to state [3][4].

**Instructions:** Standing decisions that carry across future builds. Resolving a conflict produces one automatically; you can also write instructions manually in the Instructions view. Each instruction is tied to one or more sources; when those sources change, the instruction is archived automatically [3].

## Creating a Knowledge Base

1. In the Sanity Dashboard, open **Context** and click **New knowledge base** [2].
2. Enter a **Title** and a **Purpose** (one or two sentences; the more specific, the better the outline) [2].
3. Click **Create knowledge base**, then **Add source** [2].
4. Click **Build entries**. Status reads **Entries up to date** when done. If build fails, remove failed sources and rebuild [2].
5. Review **Entries** (check topics and summaries) and **Issues** (start with Critical ones) [2].
6. Test through an agent with specific, verifiable questions [2].

Your organization's plan caps both the number of Knowledge Bases and the number of sources per Knowledge Base [2].

## Source types

A Knowledge Base requires at least one source and can combine all three types [5]:

**Dataset source**
- Documents selected by a complete GROQ query (e.g. `*[_type == "article"]{title, body}`). Bare filters are rejected [5].
- One dataset source per Knowledge Base; binds to one dataset. To switch datasets, remove and add a new source [5].
- Reads **published documents only**. A query matching nothing is rejected [5].
- Requires a role that can create datasets (Administrator or Developer by default) with unrestricted read access — a filtered read grant is not sufficient [5].
- Limit: **5,000 documents per dataset source** [5].

**Website source**
- Crawl starting from a URL. Respects `robots.txt`. Use the most specific URL possible [5].

**File source**
- Uploaded files **never re-sync**. To update, delete the import and upload the new version [5].

| Format | Maximum size |
| --- | --- |
| PDF | 500 MB |
| DOCX | 100 MB |
| PPTX | 100 MB |
| XLSX | 50 MB |
| HTML | 25 MB |
| PNG, JPEG, WebP, TIFF | 25 MB (images under 50 KB skip text extraction) |
| AsciiDoc | 25 MB |
| Markdown, plain text | Ingested directly |
| Source code, JSON, XML, CSV, TSV, YAML, and other plain-text | Ingested verbatim |
| ZIP, TAR, TAR.GZ | Expanded; each file ingested by its own format |

~40 additional text formats are also ingested verbatim. Files in unsupported formats are recorded with metadata but contents are not read. Every upload is capped at **5 GiB**; per-format limits apply first [5].

**When to upload vs. connect:** Connect as a dataset or website source for material that changes regularly. Upload for fixed material or content with no addressable source (e.g. a signed policy PDF) [5].

## Refresh schedule and maintenance

Dataset and website sources refresh on a schedule set in **Settings > Refresh interval**: **Weekly**, **Monthly**, or **Off**. New Knowledge Bases default to Weekly. Uploaded files never refresh [6].

A refresh does not automatically update entries: it recrawls sources, compares against the last build, and files issues. Entries change only when you apply those issues. While issues are open, the Knowledge Base sits in **Review** and serves entries from the last build [6].

- **Check for changes now:** Click **Check for changes** to run a refresh immediately [6].
- **After a refresh:** Agents receive refreshed content through the same outline; no agent-side change needed. If you have inlined initial context into a system prompt, refetch it after a rebuild [6].
- **Replace an uploaded file:** Delete the import and upload the new version [6].

**Refresh vs. full rebuild:**
- Refresh: files issues; applying them updates only affected entries.
- Full rebuild: reruns the whole pipeline over current sources, replaces the outline, rewrites every entry.

Rebuild when: **Rebuild required** callout appears; you changed the Knowledge Base's purpose; pipeline improvements are available; or the Knowledge Base has only uploaded files (no refresh path). Adding a new source does not need a rebuild — new material arrives as issues after upload [6].

To undo a bad build: in **Entries**, open an earlier outline version and select **Restore this version** to republish that build's entries (holds until the next build overwrites it) [6].

## Resolving issues

**Conflicts** show two claims side by side with their sources. Choose **Keep the current entry** or **Accept the incoming claim**, then click **Resolve issue**. When neither source is correct, fix the source material instead [4].

Resolution outcomes:
- "Entry is being updated now, and saved as an instruction for future rebuilds." — rewrite running as a background job.
- "Saved as an instruction that shapes your content on the next rebuild." — applies on next build [4].

**Suggested fixes** (add/remove/split/merge proposals): click **Apply**, **Dismiss**, or **Edit manually**. Issues that cannot be actioned in the app show "Manual action required" and offer only **Dismiss** and **Edit manually** [4].

**Dismissing:** Rejected without applying anything; safe to dismiss twice. Dismissed issues can be found in the dismissed filter and reopened. **Reopen and change your mind** clears the resolution and deletes the instruction it created [4].

You do not need to empty the issue queue before using a Knowledge Base. Prioritize issues marked **Critical** [4].

## Sources

1. Knowledge Bases | Sanity Docs — Web · https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases
2. Knowledge Base source types | Sanity Docs — Web · https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types
3. Create a Knowledge Base | Sanity Docs — Web · https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base
4. Resolve Knowledge Base issues | Sanity Docs — Web · https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues
5. Keep a Knowledge Base current | Sanity Docs — Web · https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base
6. Sanity Context | Sanity Docs — Web · https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context

# GROQ Queries, Schema & Studio Setup

GROQ syntax (filters, projections, sorting, slicing, references, joins, dereferencing, pipe/ellipsis operators); Sanity schema (document types, 20 built-in field types, validation rules); studio.config.js; Studio CLI quickstart.

## Studio CLI Quickstart

Initialize a new Sanity project with the CLI [1]:

```bash
npm create sanity@latest -- --dataset production --template clean --typescript --output-path studio-hello-world
cd studio-hello-world
npm run dev
```

Also supported: `pnpm create sanity@latest`, `yarn create sanity@latest`, `bun create sanity@latest`. After `npm run dev`, open `http://localhost:3333` and log in with Google, GitHub, or email (same service used during CLI login) [1].

---

## Schema (`studio.config.js`)

The top-level `schema` key in `sanity.config.js` accepts `types` (array or callback) and `templates` (array or callback for initial-value templates) [2].

### Built-in field types (20)

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `array` | Arrays of other types |
| `block` | Rich text / block content editor |
| `boolean` | True/false |
| `cross-dataset-reference` | References across datasets |
| `date` | Date only |
| `datetime` | Exact date + time |
| `document` | Top-level document type |
| `email` | Email address |
| `file` | File upload |
| `geopoint` | Geographic coordinate |
| `image` | Image upload + editing |
| `number` | Numeric value |
| `object` | Custom nested object |
| `reference` | Hard reference to another document |
| `slug` | URL slug |
| `string` | Plain string or selectable list |
| `span` | Inline text span (used within block) |
| `text` | Multi-line plain text |
| `url` | URL |
| `globalDocumentReference` | Cross-workspace document reference |

### Common field properties

- `type` *(required)*: name of a valid schema type
- `name` *(required)*: field key in the data record
- `title`: human-readable label
- `description`: hint shown to editors
- `hidden`: `boolean | () => boolean` — hides the field conditionally
- `readOnly`: `boolean | () => boolean` — prevents editing conditionally
- `deprecated`: `{ reason: string }` — renders field read-only with a deprecation message; maps to `@deprecated` in GraphQL schema
- `options`: type-specific options object
- `validation`: `RuleBuilder` — see validation methods below [2]

### Validation rules

- `Rule.required()` — field must exist
- `Rule.skip()` — discards prior rules, makes field optional (rules after still apply)
- `Rule.either([rule, rule, ...])` — passes if any rule is truthy
- `Rule.all([rule, rule, ...])` — passes only if all rules are truthy
- `Rule.custom(value, context)` — custom function; return `true` to pass, or an error string [2]

### Schema organization

All types are registered under `schema.types` in `sanity.config.js`. Recommended: keep types in a separate `schemaTypes.js` file and import them [2].

Use `defineType`, `defineField`, and `defineArrayMember` helper functions for IDE auto-suggestions and TypeScript type-safety (optional) [2]:

```js
import { defineType, defineField, defineArrayMember } from 'sanity'
export const someDocumentType = defineType({
  name: 'exampleDocumentType',
  type: 'document',
  fields: [
    defineField({
      name: 'strings', type: 'array',
      of: [defineArrayMember({ type: 'string' })]
    })
  ]
})
```

Plugins may also contribute schema types via their own `schema.types` array [2].

---

## GROQ Query Language

GROQ (Graph-Relational Object Queries) lets you describe exactly what data your application needs, joining multiple document sets and shaping the response [3].

### Basic anatomy

```groq
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979] | order(releaseYear) { _id, title, releaseYear }[0...100]
```

- `*` — every document in the dataset
- `[filter]` — filter expression; all Sanity-system fields use `_` prefix (`_type`, `_id`, etc.)
- `| order(field asc|desc)` — sort; default direction is `asc`; pipe `|` is required before `order()`
- `{ fields }` — projection; shape the returned object
- `[0...100]` — slice (0–99); `[0]` returns a single item [3]

### Projections

A projection `{_id, title}` picks only named fields. You can also declare new fields:

```groq
*[_type == 'movie']{ "directorName": director->name }
```

**Naked projection**: append `.fieldName` to get a flat array of values instead of array-of-objects:

```groq
*[_type == "movie" && references(^._id)].title  // → ["Alien", "Blade Runner", …]
```

**Ellipsis operator `...`**: include all document fields *plus* computed ones. As of GROQ API `v2021-03-25`, order matters — the last property wins when there's a conflict. Best practice: put `...` first [3].

```groq
*[_type == "movie"]{ "actorCount": count(actors), ... }
```

### References and dereferencing

- Hard reference: `{ _ref: "document-id" }` — target cannot be deleted while referenced
- Weak reference: `{ _ref: "id", _weak: true }` — does not prevent deletion
- Dereference operator `->`: follows the reference and inlines the referenced document [3]

```groq
// Single reference
*[_type == 'movie']{ director->{ name } }

// Array of references — square brackets are mandatory
*[_type == 'movie']{ producers[]-> }
```

Omitting `[]` when expanding an array of references (`producers->` instead of `producers[]->`) returns a single null value — a common gotcha [3].

### Joins and parent operator

Use a sub-query in a projection to join data. The parent operator `^` references the outer document's scope:

```groq
*[_type == "person"]{
  _id, name,
  "movies": *[_type == "movie" && references(^._id)].title
}
```

`^._id` is the `_id` of the current person; without `^`, `_id` would resolve to the inner movie document [3].

### Filtering operators

| Operator/function | Example |
|---|---|
| Comparison | `releaseYear >= 1979` |
| Boolean | `&& \|\| !` |
| Text match | `title match "Alien*"` |
| Field presence | `defined(status)` |
| Array membership | `"sci-fi" in genres` |
| References filter | `references('ridley-scott')` |

### Pipe operator `|`

Required before pipe functions (`order()`, `score()`). Optional before projections. Valid only in those contexts [3].

```groq
*[_type == "project"]{
  "status": milestones | order(year desc)[0].status
}
```

### Array traversal in projections

Use `[]` to traverse arrays and apply projections or dereferences to each member:

```groq
*[_type == "movie"]{
  "images": images[]{ caption, "url": asset->url }
}
```

### Combining queries

A projection at the top level (no leading `*`) can combine multiple independent queries into one round trip:

```groq
{
  "mainStory": *[_id == "story-1234"],
  "topStories": *[_type == "story"] | order(publishAt desc)[0..10]
}
```

This is useful for loading all content needed for a page in a single cacheable request [3].

## Sources

2. Setting up your studio | Sanity Docs — Web · https://www.sanity.io/docs/astro-quickstart/setting-up-your-studio
3. How GROQ Queries Work - Step by Step Guide | Sanity Docs — Web · https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work
